summary.text: At \(p=11\), the quadratic character used in the statement is \((7/11)=-1\), so its proposed right-hand side is \(-55\equiv66\pmod{121}\). Direct evaluation of the finite weighted sum gives \(44\pmod{121}\), contradicting the claimed congruence (and revealing that the accepted disproof relies on the character’s arguments being reversed from \((11/7)\)).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj^2\binom{n-j}{j}^2(-16)^j
\]
and
\[
W(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k).
\]
The accepted argument specializes the asserted universal congruence to the prime
\(p=11\). Since \(11\neq 7\), this is an admissible specialization.

There is, however, an essential notation issue. The symbol used in the accepted formal statement is the Legendre symbol with numerator \(7\) and prime denominator \(p\), namely
\[
L(p)=\left(\frac{7}{p}\right).
\]
Thus the statement actually refuted by the argument is
\[
W(p)\equiv p\left(21\left(\frac7p\right)+16\right)\pmod{p^2}.
\tag{1}
\]
This is not the same as the canonical OEIS statement displayed in the question, whose symbol is \(\left(\frac p7\right)\). The counterexample calculation is as follows.

For \(0\leq k\leq 10\), direct evaluation of the defining finite binomial sums gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
k&a(k)\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&1\\
2&-63\\
3&-575\\
4&6913\\
5&224001\\
6&420801\\
7&-69020223\\
8&-918270975\\
9&14596918273\\
10&511845045697
\end{array}
\]
For example,
\[
a(2)=\binom20^2\binom20^2+
\binom21^2\binom11^2(-16)+
\binom22^2\binom02^2(-16)^2
=1-64=-63.
\]
The remaining entries are obtained in exactly the same way by expanding the finite sum; terms with \(j>n-j\) vanish because \(\binom{n-j}{j}=0\).

Multiplying these values by their weights \((42k+37)(-1)^k\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
k&(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k)&\text{residue modulo }121\\ \hline
0&37&37\\
1&-79&42\\
2&-7623&0\\
3&93725&71\\
4&1417165&13\\
5&-55328247&92\\
6&121611489&76\\
7&22845693813&107\\
8&-342515073675&94\\
9&-6057721083295&31\\
10&233913185883529&86
\end{array}
\]
Consequently
\[
W(11)=227535863206839.
\]
Indeed,
\[
227535863206839=121\cdot1880461679395+44,
\]
so
\[
W(11)\equiv44\pmod{121}.
\tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, summing the residues in the last column gives
\[
37+42+0+71+13+92+76+107+94+31+86=649=5\cdot121+44.
\]

We next evaluate the Legendre symbol occurring in (1). The nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(11\) are obtained by squaring \(1,2,3,4,5\):
\[
1^2\equiv1,\qquad 2^2\equiv4,\qquad 3^2\equiv9,
\qquad4^2\equiv5,\qquad5^2\equiv3\pmod{11}.
\]
Hence the set of nonzero squares modulo \(11\) is
\(\{1,3,4,5,9\}\). It does not contain \(7\), so \(7\) is a quadratic nonresidue modulo \(11\), and therefore
\[
\left(\frac7{11}\right)=-1.
\tag{3}
\]
The right-hand side of (1) at \(p=11\) is consequently
\[
11\left(21\left(\frac7{11}\right)+16\right)
=11(-21+16)=-55.
\]
Modulo \(121\), this is
\[
-55\equiv66\pmod{121}.
\tag{4}
\]
Equations (2) and (4) are incompatible: \(44\not\equiv66\pmod{121}\), because their difference is \(22\), which is not divisible by \(121\). Thus (1) fails for the prime \(p=11\), disproving the universally quantified formal variant used in the accepted argument.

For completeness, this does not disprove the canonical conjecture as written in the question. In that conjecture the relevant symbol at \(p=11\) is instead
\[
\left(\frac{11}{7}\right)=\left(\frac47\right)=1,
\]
because \(4\equiv2^2\pmod7\). Its right-hand side is then
\[
11(21\cdot1+16)=11\cdot37=407\equiv44\pmod{121},
\]
which agrees exactly with (2). Therefore the accepted construction is a valid counterexample to the statement with \(\left(\frac7p\right)\), but it is not a counterexample to the canonical OEIS congruence with \(\left(\frac p7\right)\). The apparent disproof results from reversing the two arguments of the Legendre symbol.
